0.title: Ecclesiastes: Fear God and Keep His Commandments
0.overview:
Ecclesiastes is a deeply honest book about life in a fallen world. It asks the questions people think in the night and rarely say aloud: what is the point of all this work, why the wicked prosper, why pleasure fades, what happens when we die. It makes the reader feel their full weight, and then it points him to God.

The speaker is called the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem (1:1). The description fits Solomon, the wisest and richest king Israel ever had. If anyone could have made life work on its own terms, it was he.

Was the Preacher Solomon? The traditional view holds that Solomon wrote it, perhaps late in life; the description fits only him, and the words I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem (1:12) claim his experience. Many scholars, including some conservative ones, hold that a later wise man wrote in Solomon’s person, pointing to 1:16, all who were over Jerusalem before me, when only David had reigned there before him as king of Israel, and to the book’s late Hebrew, which includes a word borrowed from Persian (parks, 2:5). Defenders of Solomon’s authorship reply that Jerusalem had kings long before David, such as Melchizedek and Adoni-zedek (Gen 14:18; Josh 10:1), and that wording can be updated in copying. The book does not name Solomon, the question remains debated, and certainty is not possible. One careful reading is that it gives us Solomon’s own search, set down and framed by a later voice (12:9–14); either way, its authority rests on the God who gave it (12:11), not on the human name.

Two phrases run through the book. Under the sun, twenty-eight times in the ESV, is the Preacher's vantage point: life as anyone can observe it, from the level of the world. Vanity translates hebel, which the ESV notes means a "mist", a "vapor" or a "mere breath"; it appears five times in 1:2 and in twenty-nine other verses. The verdict All is vanity (1:2) does not first mean that life is worthless. It means that everything under the sun is breath: real, and impossible to hold.

So the book's great question is What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? (1:3). The Preacher tests pleasure, achievement, wealth and wisdom, and finds that none of them can outlast death (2:1-17). Under the sun alone, there is no final gain.

But two other threads are the book's heart. The first is joy. Again and again the Preacher says there is nothing better than to eat, drink and find enjoyment in one's work, because This also, I saw, is from the hand of God (2:24; see also 3:12-13, 22; 5:18-20; 8:15; 9:7-10; 11:7-10). What cannot be seized from the world can be received from God. The second is the fear of God (3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12-13), which becomes the book's final word: Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man (12:13). The book never uses the covenant name LORD; it speaks of God, the Creator whom every person must reckon with.

Another voice frames the book. Someone speaks about the Preacher (says the Preacher, 1:2; 7:27; 12:8) and at the end commends his words and draws the conclusion (12:9-14). The Preacher's words are given by one Shepherd (12:11). So the hard sayings are not the last word on their own: the book leads the reader through honest despair to the fear of God.

The New Testament shows where Ecclesiastes leads. Creation was indeed subjected to futility, but in hope (Rom 8:20): the hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Rom 8:21), anchored in Christ’s resurrection. The Preacher asked what gain there is in toil; Paul could say, in the Lord your labor is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58). The Preacher asked, Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward? (3:21); Christ abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10). The wisest son of David asked the questions, and Jesus said, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt 12:42). Many Christians hear in that one Shepherd the voice of the one who said, I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

1.title: Vanity of Vanities: What Does Man Gain?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Verdict and the Endless Round
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem (v. 1). His verdict comes first: Vanity of vanities, All is vanity (v. 2), and his question second: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? (v. 3). Generations, sun, wind and streams all move and never arrive (vv. 4-7). Eye and ear are never satisfied (v. 8), there is nothing new under the sun (v. 9), and no one is remembered (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Life seen only from under the sun is motion without arrival, and the book makes us feel that before it shows us any way out.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book opens with a title rather than a name. The ESV calls the speaker the Preacher, and its footnote gives the Hebrew word, Qoheleth, with two other possible renderings: "Convener" or "Collector". He is someone who gathers: he gathers people to listen, and he gathers sayings, weighing and studying and arranging many proverbs with great care (12:9). The word "Preacher" catches the first sense well. This is a man speaking to an assembly about the most serious questions a human being can ask.

He is the son of David, king in Jerusalem. The book never names Solomon, and it may be that it is not meant to be read as his signature so much as in his voice. But the description fits only one son of David who reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel (v. 12), the king of whom it is written, God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure (1 Kgs 4:29). That is the point. The man about to say that everything under the sun is vanity is not a failure grumbling in a corner. He is the richest, wisest, most successful man of his age. If anyone could have made life under the sun work, it was he.

Something greater than Solomon is here, Jesus said (Matt 12:42). The wisest son of David asks the question, and the greater Son of David is the answer.
verseByVerse.note: “The Preacher” translates Qoheleth, which may also mean “Convener” or “Collector” (ESV note) — one who gathers an assembly. The “son of David, king in Jerusalem” points to Solomon, though he is not named.

verseByVerse.quote: Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a single argument, the verdict. Vanity of vanities is built like "king of kings" or "holy of holies": vanity at its utmost, said twice.

The word is hebel, a "mist" or "mere breath" (see the note), and it is the key to the whole book. All is vanity does not first say that everything is worthless. It says that everything is breath: real, as your breath on a cold morning is real, but grasp it and your hand closes on nothing.

That is a more precise and more painful diagnosis than "life is pointless". Work, pleasure, wisdom, wealth, reputation and youth are breath. None of them can bear the weight of a soul that leans its whole life on them. James uses the same picture for life itself: For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes (Jas 4:14).

The phrase says the Preacher is spoken about him, not by him. That voice is heard again in 7:27 and at the end (12:8-14), and it frames the whole book.
verseByVerse.note: “Vanity” translates hebel: literally a mist, vapor or mere breath — something fleeting (ESV note). It appears five times in this verse and in 29 other verses of the book.

verseByVerse.quote: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the question that drives the book. Gain is what is left over when everything is added up. After a lifetime of work, what do you have that lasts?

Toil is the whole effort of a life, with the sweat that God spoke of to Adam: cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life (Gen 3:17). Under the sun is the Preacher's vantage point: life on the level of the world as anyone can see it. What can be proved from there alone?

His answer, for now, is nothing, and if this life is all there is, he is right. Jesus asked the same question in sharper form: For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? (Matt 16:26).

After Christ rose from the dead, Paul could write the sentence that answers verse 3: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58). Ecclesiastes does not yet say that. It makes us need it.
verseByVerse.note: “Under the sun” — life viewed from this world alone — occurs 28 times in the book.

verseByVerse.quote: A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to the place where it rises. The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A generation goes. Stand in a cemetery and read the dates: generation after generation walked these streets, and the streets outlasted them. Man was made to rule the earth, and the earth outlives man.

The sun rises. Psalm 19 sees the sun as a strong man who runs its course with joy (Ps 19:5). The Preacher feels its weariness: hastens may be rendered "returns panting" (ESV note), back round to do it all again.

Wind and streams. Every part of creation is busy, and none of it arrives. This is the world as a treadmill, and human toil has the same shape: you get up, work, sleep, and do it again, and the inbox fills back up.

Is this how God sees the world? Not finally. The same sun knows its time for setting because God appointed it (Ps 104:19). Paul says creation really was subjected to futility after the fall, but because of him who subjected it, in hope (Rom 8:20). The treadmill is real. It is also not the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: All things are full of weariness; a man cannot utter it; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the weariness moves inside. The world is tiring, and it is also more tiring than words can say: a man cannot utter it. And the human appetite that should rest in what it takes in never does. The eye is not satisfied with seeing. Scroll through another hundred images and the eye wants the next one. Hear the new song and the ear is already waiting for another.

Proverbs says the same with a darker comparison: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man (Prov 27:20). The grave is never full, and neither is the human heart. We were made with an appetite that nothing under the sun can fill.

That is not a defect in us; it is a clue. Jesus stood by a well and said, Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again (John 4:13-14). Of anything you hope will finally satisfy, ask: has anything like it ever satisfied you for long?

verseByVerse.quote: What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun. Is there a thing of which it is said, "See, this is new"? It has been already in the ages before us. There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be any remembrance of later things yet to be among those who come after.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing new. Technology changes; the human story does not. The same pride, lust, greed and grief are acted out in every generation with new props. Point to the latest thing, and it has been done before. The claim to be new is itself very old.

Only one voice in Scripture can truly say it. At the end of the Bible, the one seated on the throne says, Behold, I am making all things new (Rev 21:5). Newness does not come up from under the sun. It comes down, and it has already begun: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come (2 Cor 5:17).

There is no remembrance. The ESV notes that former things and later things may be rendered "former people" and "later people". Either way, you will be forgotten. Try naming your great-great-grandparents. Under the sun, even the memory of a life is breath. The comfort of the believer is that he is not remembered by history, but by God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — The King Who Searched and Found Sorrow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem, and he set his heart to search out by wisdom everything done under heaven (vv. 12-13). What he found was vanity and a striving after wind; the crooked cannot be straightened (vv. 14-15). He had great wisdom and studied madness and folly as well (vv. 16-17), and learned that in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom can see how broken the world is, but it cannot mend it. Only the one who made the world can make the crooked straight.

verseByVerse.quote: I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem. And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.
verseByVerse.commentary:
King over Israel. Having shown us the world, the Preacher now tells us his own story. He writes as a man who had every advantage for the search he is about to describe: a throne, a capital city, wealth, time and the best minds of the kingdom at his call.

I applied my heart. The ESV's note explains that the Hebrew term for heart denotes the centre of a person's inner life, including mind, will and emotions. This was not an idle hobby. He gave himself, all of himself, to understanding life. He did it by wisdom, the best tool human beings have.

An unhappy business. And here God is named for the first time in the book. It is God who has given this business, and the Preacher calls it unhappy. That is honest. The drive to understand our lives is itself a burden, because we ask questions we cannot answer. Yet he does not say there is no God. He says God has laid this weight on us, and he feels it. Faith in Ecclesiastes is not the absence of hard questions. It is holding on to God while asking them.

verseByVerse.quote: I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind. What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Striving after wind. The verdict of verse 2, with a new picture: "a feeding on wind" (ESV note), as in Hosea, where Ephraim feeds on the wind and pursues the east wind all day long (Hos 12:1). Try to live on wind, and you starve.

What is crooked. Wisdom can diagnose, but it cannot cure. It can see that a marriage is bent, a nation corrupt, a heart twisted, and it cannot straighten them or add back what is missing. The Preacher will name who bent it: Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked? (7:13). The answer is that no man can, but God can. When John the Baptist prepared the way for Christ, the promise was that the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways (Luke 3:5). What wisdom cannot mend, the Lord who came can.

Think of the thing you have tried longest to straighten. Verse 15 is not despair. It is permission to stop pretending you can fix it alone, and to bring it to him.
verseByVerse.note: “Striving after wind” may be rendered “a feeding on wind” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, "I have acquired great wisdom, surpassing all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge." And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also is but a striving after wind. For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great wisdom. He is not boasting idly. Solomon was wiser than all other men (1 Kgs 4:31), and he lays out his credentials so that his conclusion cannot be dismissed. He studied wisdom and folly alike, like someone reading every philosophy on the shelf for the key, and even that was chasing wind.

Much vexation. The more you know, the more it hurts. The child is happy in the car because he does not know about the mortgage. The doctor knows what the shadow on the scan means. Knowledge without redemption is a sharper pain.

So Paul says that the world did not know God through wisdom, and it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe (1 Cor 1:21). Human wisdom climbs the ladder and finds only sorrow at the top. God comes down, and takes the sorrow on himself. The one who knew every heart and every grief was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief (Isa 53:3). He increased in knowledge, and carried the sorrow of it, so that those who come to him might find in him what the Preacher could not find under the sun: Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30).

1.overview:
The Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem, opens with his verdict: All is vanity (vv. 1-2). The word means mist or breath, something real but impossible to hold. Then comes the question the whole book is asking: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? (v. 3).

The world is an endless round. Generations come and go, the sun rises and sets, the wind circles and the streams run to a sea that is never full (vv. 4-7). The eye and ear are never satisfied, nothing is new, and nobody is remembered (vv. 8-11).

The Preacher then tells his own story. As king he set his heart to search out everything under heaven by wisdom (vv. 12-13). He found that all is a striving after wind, that the crooked cannot be made straight, and that increasing knowledge only increases sorrow (vv. 14-18).
1.theology:
Life viewed only under the sun yields no lasting gain (v. 3). Creation has been subjected to futility since the fall, but in hope of being set free (Rom 8:20-21), and the Preacher never says that there is no God; he says that God has given this burden (v. 13).

Human wisdom can diagnose what is crooked but cannot straighten it (v. 15; 7:13). God does what wisdom cannot: the crooked is made straight in the coming of Christ (Luke 3:5), who makes all things new (Rev 21:5; 2 Cor 5:17), and in whom labour is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58).

The restless eye (v. 8) shows that people are made for more than the world can give (John 4:13-14). The wisest son of David asks the question; something greater than Solomon is its answer (Matt 12:42; 1 Cor 1:30).
1.examples:
Your breath on a cold morning: visible, real, and gone when you try to grasp it.

Reading the dates in a cemetery.

The inbox that fills back up.

Scrolling for the next image.

Trying to name your great-great-grandparents.

The child happy in the car, and the parent who knows about the mortgage.

2.title: The King's Experiment: Pleasure, Greatness and the Hand of God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Experiment with Pleasure and Greatness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher tests his heart with pleasure and finds it vanity (vv. 1-2). He tries wine while keeping his wisdom, and then builds on a royal scale: houses, vineyards, gardens, pools, slaves, herds, silver and gold, singers (vv. 3-8). He surpasses all before him and denies his eyes nothing (vv. 9-10). Then he looks at it all: behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who had everything the world can offer is the best witness that the world cannot satisfy.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself." But behold, this also was vanity. I said of laughter, "It is mad," and of pleasure, "What use is it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A test of pleasure. Chapter 1 ended with more knowledge bringing more sorrow, so the Preacher tries the obvious alternative: if thinking hurts, start enjoying. It is a deliberate test, and the result is recorded before the method: this also was vanity.

Laughter. Laughter is good; the Preacher is not a killjoy, as the end of this chapter will prove. But laughter pursued as the meaning of life is mad. Everyone knows the party where the laughter gets louder as the evening goes on and emptier with every glass. Pleasure asks to be taken as an answer, and when it is questioned, What use is it?, it has nothing to say.

Our culture has run this experiment on a vast scale, and the result has not changed. Paul's description of the last days includes people who are lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God (2 Tim 3:4). Pleasure is a wonderful gift and a cruel god.

verseByVerse.quote: I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine—my heart still guiding me with wisdom—and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is not a man falling into drunkenness but a scientist experimenting on himself, my heart still guiding me with wisdom. He wants to know one thing: what is actually good for the children of man to do in the few days of their life?

Life is short, and Moses prayed, So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom (Ps 90:12).

There is a warning here too. Many have told themselves they could taste folly while keeping their head. Most cannot. The prodigal son also went looking for life in a far country and squandered his property in reckless living (Luke 15:13).

verseByVerse.quote: I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself. I made myself gardens and parks, and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees. I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees. I bought male and female slaves, and had slaves who were born in my house. I had also great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem. I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, both men and women, and many concubines, the delight of the sons of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great works. Now achievement. Listen to the repeated words: I made, I built, for myself, I made myself. He builds a private paradise, as if he were trying to build Eden again with his own hands.

Slaves, silver and singers. Then people, livestock, money, art and sex. The meaning of the word behind many concubines is uncertain (ESV note), but the phrase that follows is clear: the delight of the sons of man. He had every delight.

Scripture records that King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom (1 Kgs 10:23). This list is the modern dream fully achieved. Most people never get it, and imagine that if they did, they would be satisfied. The Preacher got it.

Does the Bible approve his slaves and concubines? No. It records them as a king’s excess, not as a model. The law told Israel’s king not to multiply wives or silver and gold (Deut 17:17), and Solomon’s wives turned away his heart after other gods (1 Kgs 11:4). Slavery in Israel was a regulated institution of a fallen world, not God’s design; the gospel makes slave and free one in Christ (Gal 3:28) and condemns man-stealing (1 Tim 1:10). And the garden he built for himself could not bring back Eden. Only Christ opens paradise again (Luke 23:43), where the tree of life stands by the river of God (Rev 22:1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me. And whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my reward for all my toil. Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I became great. He reached the top. And he kept his head while doing it. The experiment was not spoiled by a man who lost his judgment on the way up.

And whatever my eyes. He is honest: it was enjoyable. My heart found pleasure in all my toil. There was real satisfaction in the building and the owning. But see the limit of it: this was my reward. The pleasure of the work was all the work paid. Once the enjoyment was spent, nothing was left over.

Then I considered. Then comes the moment every achiever meets. Everything he dreamed of stands finished in front of him, and he feels nothing. The athlete stands on the podium and wonders why it is not enough. The executive reaches the corner office and lies awake.

Jesus told of a rich man who did exactly what the Preacher did, and said to his soul, relax, eat, drink, be merry. But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?' (Luke 12:19-20). Moses saw the same truth from the other side, choosing the people of God rather than the fleeting pleasures of sin, for he was looking to the reward (Heb 11:25-26).

Ask it plainly of your own ambitions: if you had all of it, what would you have?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Wise and Fool Die Alike
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He turns to weigh wisdom against folly (v. 12). Wisdom really is better, as there is more gain in light than in darkness (vv. 13-14), And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them. The wise man dies like the fool and is forgotten like him (vv. 15-16), so I hated life (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom is better than folly for living, but under the sun it cannot answer death.

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly. For what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done. Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness. The wise person has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom and madness. Pleasure failed, so he weighs wisdom. No one after him can run the experiment on a bigger scale: if a king with unlimited resources found it empty, no one else need try.

More gain in wisdom. The Preacher is not against wisdom. A wise person sees where he is walking; the fool walks into walls. Every word of Proverbs stands. Wisdom brings real gain, the same word as 1:3, for living.

And yet. Wisdom helps you walk through life. It cannot stop the road from ending in the same place. The same event, which he will name in a moment, is death. The wise and the fool walk different roads to the same grave.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said in my heart, "What happens to the fool will happen to me also. Why then have I been so very wise?" And I said in my heart that this also is vanity. For of the wise as of the fool there is no enduring remembrance, seeing that in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. How the wise dies just like the fool! So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why so very wise? The question becomes personal. He spent his life becoming wise, the fool across the street did nothing, and both will be buried. It is the question of the student who worked hard beside the one who never did, and then watched both fail the same exam.

No enduring remembrance. Not only death, but forgetting; the cry is almost a lament. Psalm 49 says the same: For he sees that even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish and leave their wealth to others (Ps 49:10).

So I hated life. The Preacher does not pretend. Some readers know what it is to lie awake and feel exactly this, and it matters that God put these words in his book. You are not the first believer to feel it, and the feeling is not the end of the story. If it has become a wish not to live, tell someone you trust today and seek help at once; God gives doctors, friends and pastors for such nights.

He hated life under the sun, life seen from that level alone. That is the qualifier to hold onto. Everything under the sun ends in death. But God has not left us under the sun alone: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27), and Christ came to deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:15).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He hates his toil, because he must leave it to someone who may be a fool (vv. 18-19). He gives his heart up to despair: a person who toiled with skill leaves everything to someone who never worked for it (vv. 20-21). For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything gathered for self is finally handed to someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: I hated all my toil in which I toil under the sun, seeing that I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything he built will be left to someone he cannot control. A man spends forty years building a business, and his heir sells it in three. A woman saves carefully all her life, and the estate is fought over by relatives she barely knew.

For a son of David these words are painful. Solomon's own son Rehoboam came to the throne and answered the people harshly, and forsaking the counsel that the old men had given him (1 Kgs 12:13), and the kingdom his father had built was torn in two. Who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Solomon did not know. Nobody does.

Man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather! (Ps 39:6). The only safe inheritance is one that cannot be squandered: lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal (Matt 6:20).

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned about and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil of my labors under the sun, because sometimes a person who has toiled with wisdom and knowledge and skill must leave everything to be enjoyed by someone who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil. What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun? For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Despair. The Preacher reaches the bottom, and calls it a great evil. It is wrong that skill and wisdom and years of labour should be handed to someone who did nothing. Under the sun, there is no justice in inheritance.

What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun? The question of 1:3 returns, and this time with the cost added. Work done for self alone consumes the worker. His days are sorrow, his work is vexation, and Even in the night his heart does not rest. Anyone who has lain awake in the small hours running through the numbers knows this verse.

The psalmist names the cure: It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep (Ps 127:2). The sleepless night is not a sign that you care enough. It is often a sign that you are carrying what only God can carry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–26 — Nothing Better: From the Hand of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God (v. 24), for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment? (v. 25). God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him, and the sinner gathers for someone else (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: Joy cannot be seized from the world; it is received from the hand of God.

verseByVerse.quote: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God, for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing better. And then, suddenly, light. This is the first of several such passages in the book (3:12-13, 22; 5:18-20; 8:15; 9:7-10), and they are the thread of hope running through it.

What has changed? One phrase: from the hand of God. The experiment of verses 1-11 tried to seize enjoyment from the world, and it evaporated. Here enjoyment is received from God as a gift, and it is good. The same bread and wine, the same work, taste different when they come from a Father's hand. The ESV notes that find enjoyment may be rendered "make his soul see good": God opens the soul's eyes to the good that is in front of it.

This is not the rich fool's eat, drink, be merry, which leaves God out. It is Paul's God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Tim 6:17), and whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God (1 Cor 10:31).

for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment? Without God, no one can truly enjoy anything; the rich man with every delight could not. Most Hebrew manuscripts read "apart from me"; the ESV follows others in reading apart from him, which makes the point directly: enjoyment is God's to give. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above (Jas 1:17). Tonight's supper can be received that way.

verseByVerse.quote: For to the one who pleases him God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to one who pleases God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two people, two gifts. To the one who pleases God, wisdom and knowledge and joy: the very things the king could not get by his own effort. To the sinner, busyness, only to hand it over to someone else. Proverbs has the same pattern: the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous (Prov 13:22).

Who pleases God? Not the one who earns it, but the one who trusts him. The New Testament is clear that without faith it is impossible to please him (Heb 11:6), and the joy offered here is the joy of a person who has stopped trying to wring meaning out of the world and received it from God.

The closing refrain probably refers to the sinner's gathering. But it also keeps the reader honest: even God's good gifts under the sun are breath. They are good, and they are not God. So the psalmist: Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Ps 73:25).

2.overview:
The Preacher tests his heart with pleasure and laughter and finds them vanity (vv. 1-3). He builds houses, gardens and pools, gathers slaves, herds, silver, gold and singers, and becomes greater than all before him; yet when he looks at everything, all was vanity and a striving after wind (vv. 4-11).

Wisdom is better than folly, as light is better than darkness, but the wise and the fool die alike and are forgotten, and he hates life (vv. 12-17). He hates his toil because he must leave it to someone who may be a fool, and his days are sorrow and his nights restless (vv. 18-23).

Then comes the first ray of light: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God (v. 24). God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him (vv. 25-26).
2.theology:
Pleasure and achievement pursued as the meaning of life cannot satisfy (vv. 1-11; Luke 12:15-21). Wisdom is genuinely better than folly, but it cannot overcome death (vv. 13-16; Ps 49:10); only Christ delivers from the fear of death (Heb 2:14-15).

Enjoyment is a gift from the hand of God, not a prize seized from the world (vv. 24-25; Jas 1:17; 1 Tim 6:17). The same things that are vanity when made ultimate become good when received from God with thanksgiving (1 Tim 4:4). God gives joy to those who please him, and the sinner's gathering passes to others (v. 26; Prov 13:22).
2.examples:
The party that gets louder and emptier as the evening goes on.

The athlete on the podium who wonders why it is not enough.

A business built over forty years and sold by the heir in three.

Lying awake in the small hours running through the numbers.

The same supper, received as a gift from a Father's hand.

3.title: A Time for Everything, and Eternity in the Heart

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — A Time for Every Matter Under Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven (v. 1). Fourteen pairs follow, from birth and death, planting and uprooting (v. 2), through killing and healing, weeping and laughing, mourning and dancing (vv. 3-4), gathering and casting away, seeking and losing, tearing and sewing, silence and speech (vv. 5-7), to a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Every moment of a human life has its appointed time, and the one who appoints the times is God.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:
verseByVerse.commentary:
This passage is usually heard as gentle poetry about the rhythms of life. In the Preacher's mouth it is something stronger. Chapter 1 showed the world going round and round; chapter 3 shows that the round is not random. Every event in a human life has its appointed moment, and the chapter makes clear who appointed it: He has made everything beautiful in its time (v. 11).

That can feel like a cage or a comfort, depending on who you believe sets the times. The psalmist, surrounded by enemies, found it a comfort: My times are in your hand (Ps 31:15).

Does “a time for everything” mean fatalism? It is wisdom about discerning the right moment: there is a time to plant and a time to uproot, and the wise know which. God appoints the times (v. 11), and we are still responsible for how we act in them.

verseByVerse.quote: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted; a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Born and die. The list begins at the edges of life, two appointments no one chooses. Then the farmer's year: plant in the wrong season and the crop is lost, however hard you work. The fourteen pairs of opposites cover the whole of life, the way "day and night" means all the time.

A time to kill. This is not a licence for private violence. Scripture gives the sword to rightful authority, for justice: Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed (Gen 9:6), and the ruler does not bear the sword in vain (Rom 13:4). There is a time when justice or defence requires it, and a time when healing is called for.

Break down and build up belong together too. A rotten house must sometimes come down before a sound one is built; so with habits, churches and hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weep and laugh. The Christian life is not a permanent smile. Jesus wept at the grave of his friend. Wisdom is knowing which room you are in. Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). Telling a grieving friend to cheer up is not faith. It is getting the time wrong.

Stones. The meaning of casting away and gathering stones is not certain; it may picture clearing a field and collecting stones for a wall. Set beside embracing and refraining, it suggests coming close and holding back: a time to hold someone near and a time to let them go.

verseByVerse.quote: a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seek and lose. There is a time to look for what is lost, and a time to accept that it is gone. Anyone who has emptied a parent's house after a death knows both halves in a single afternoon.

Tear and sew. Tearing a garment was the sign of grief in Israel; sewing is the work of mending. Job's friends did best in the first seven days, when they said nothing, and there are also moments when silence is cowardice.

Love and hate. A time to hate startles us, but Scripture does not ask us to feel nothing about evil. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good (Rom 12:9). The psalmist could say, Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? (Ps 139:21). A person who cannot hate cruelty does not truly love its victims.

And the list ends with peace, toward which God is bringing history. The time the whole Bible looks toward is the fullness of time, when God sent forth his Son (Gal 4:4). Jesus lived by his Father's times: My hour has not yet come (John 2:4), and at the end, Father, the hour has come (John 17:1). At the right time Christ died for the ungodly (Rom 5:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What gain has the worker from his toil? (v. 9). God has given the business of life (v. 10). He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet man cannot find out the whole of God's work (v. 11). So there is nothing better than to be joyful, to do good, and to receive food and work as God's gift to man (vv. 12-13). What God does endures forever, so that people fear before him (v. 14), and God seeks what has been driven away (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: We are made for eternity and cannot see it whole; God's gifts are to be received now, and God himself feared.

verseByVerse.quote: What gain has the worker from his toil? I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What gain has the worker from his toil? After the poem, the question of 1:3 again. If God has set every time, what can our work add? We cannot change the seasons. We plant when it is time to plant and die when it is time to die. So where is the gain?

The business God has given. In 1:13 he called it unhappy; here he simply says God has given it. The work of life is not an accident but an assignment, and the one who assigned it knows why.

verseByVerse.quote: He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beautiful in its time. Even weeping, losing and dying. A funeral is not beautiful as a funeral, but set in the whole design it has a place. Think of a tapestry seen from behind: knots and loose threads; turn it over and the picture appears. Joseph lived more than twenty years on the wrong side of it, and at the end he could say to his brothers, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20). We know that for those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28).

Eternity in the heart. Here is why human beings cannot be content with the treadmill of chapter 1. Animals do not ask what their life means. People do. We long for love not to end, for justice to be done, for the dead not to be lost. That longing was put there by God, and it is why nothing under the sun satisfies. The KJV reads he hath set the world in their heart, but the Hebrew word usually means a long or unending time, as most modern translations take it.

But the same verse sets a limit. We have eternity in the heart and a few decades in the hand: we sense the shape of the whole and cannot see it. Only God is declaring the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10). So we live, as Paul says, seeing in a mirror dimly, but then face to face (1 Cor 13:12).

The longing for eternity is finally a longing for God. The eternal Son entered our few decades, so that people with eternity in their hearts and dust in their bodies could have eternal life in him (John 17:3). He said, I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25).

verseByVerse.quote: I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live; also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in all his toil—this is God's gift to man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing better. If we cannot see the whole, what should we do? The Preacher's answer is the second of his "nothing better" passages (2:24). Be joyful, and do good. Two simple things, and they belong together. Joy without doing good is selfish; doing good without joy is grim. As long as they live: not someday, when the whole picture makes sense, but now.

God's gift to man. Meals, drink, daily work. A person who cannot see how his life fits together can still sit at his table tonight and thank God for the bread. That is the life of faith in its daily form. For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Tim 4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him. That which is, already has been; that which is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Endures forever. Human work evaporates; God's work stands, and no one can improve on it or undo it. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa 40:8).

God's purpose is stated: so that people fear before him. This is the first mention of the fear of God in the book, and it is where the book will end (12:13). When a person sees that his own work is breath and God's is permanent, the right response is reverent awe. The fear of God is not terror before a tyrant. It is taking God seriously as God.

What has been driven away. The first half echoes 1:9; the second is new. The Hebrew is "what has been pursued" (ESV note). The past seems chased away by time, but God goes after it and calls it to account, which is probably the Preacher's main point: nothing done in time escapes God.

Many Christians have also heard in the words a wider truth, the heart of God throughout Scripture: I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed (Ezek 34:16). And it is the mission of his Son: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). If you feel driven away, you are exactly the kind of person God seeks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — Injustice, Judgment and the Dust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wickedness sits even in the place of justice (v. 16), but God will judge the righteous and the wicked (v. 17). God tests people to show them they are like beasts: All are from the dust, and to dust all return (vv. 18-20). Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward? (v. 21). So a man should rejoice in his work, for no one can show him what comes after (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Under the sun, man and beast die alike; above the sun, God will judge, and the spirit returns to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness. I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The place of justice. From the beauty of God's times to human injustice, found in the worst place: the courtroom. When the judge is corrupt, where can the wronged go?

God will judge. Here he rises above the sun. The poem named no time for judgment, and here it is: the verdict too has its time. The corrupt judge has his day in court coming.

The New Testament names the day and the judge: God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). For the oppressed, that is the best news there is. For all of us, it is a reason to flee to the judge while he is offering mercy, for the one who will judge is the one who died for sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts. For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity. All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the beasts. When people devour one another like animals, God lets them see what they are without him. Pride says, we are the masters of the world. Death answers, you are creatures. Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish (Ps 49:20).

One breath. From under the sun, this is simply true: a man and a dog both stop breathing. When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust (Ps 104:29).

All go to one place. The grave, as God said to Adam: for you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19). The Preacher wants his hearers to feel it, because only a person who knows he is dust will look to God for life.

verseByVerse.quote: Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
From under the sun, no one can prove what happens after death. The Preacher does not deny that the spirit goes upward; he says observation cannot settle it. But he will say at the end that the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it (12:7). What sight cannot establish, God has revealed.

And someone has come back. Christ Jesus abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10). Paul knew where the believer's spirit goes: we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8). The dying thief heard it from Christ himself: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). The question "Who knows?" has an answer, and his name is Jesus.

The ESV notes that the verse may be rendered Who knows the spirit of man, which goes upward, close to the KJV, which reads it as a statement that the spirit does go upward. Does verse 20, All go to one place, mean that the dead simply cease, or sleep unaware until the resurrection? Some sincere Christians have read this verse and 9:5 that way, wanting to honour the plain words. But the Preacher describes what can be seen: the body goes to the grave like an animal's. This commentary holds, with the Westminster Confession (32.1) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (31.1), that the souls of believers go at death to be with Christ, awake and at rest, awaiting the resurrection of the body (Phil 1:23).

verseByVerse.quote: So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since you cannot see or control what comes after you, rejoice in his work: it is your lot, the share God has assigned.

This is not resignation but freedom. The person who must see how everything turns out will never be at peace. The person who does today's work gladly as his portion from God, and leaves the future with God, can rest. Paul put it this way: Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward (Col 3:23-24).

3.overview:
For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven (v. 1). Fourteen pairs of opposites, from birth and death to war and peace, cover the whole of life and show that every moment has its appointed time (vv. 2-8).

God has made everything beautiful in its time and put eternity into man's heart, so his gifts are to be received with joy and he is to be feared (vv. 9-15). Wickedness sits in the place of justice, but God will judge; man and beast die alike, and no one under the sun can see what follows (vv. 16-22).
3.theology:
God appoints every time of human life (vv. 1-8; Ps 31:15) and makes everything beautiful in its time (v. 11; Rom 8:28). He has set eternity in the human heart, so that nothing temporal can satisfy, while keeping the whole of his purpose beyond our sight (v. 11; Isa 46:10; 1 Cor 13:12).

God's work endures and is meant to produce reverent fear (v. 14). God seeks what has been driven away (v. 15; Luke 19:10). He will judge the righteous and the wicked (v. 17), and has fixed the day by the risen Christ (Acts 17:31).

Under the sun, man dies like the beasts (vv. 18-20; Gen 3:19). The question of v. 21 is answered in 12:7 and fully in the gospel, which has brought life and immortality to light (2 Tim 1:10).
3.examples:
The farmer who plants in the wrong season.

Telling a grieving friend to cheer up.

Emptying a parent's house in a single afternoon.

A tapestry seen from behind.

The bribed judge who has his own day in court coming.

Tomorrow morning's work, done as your lot from God.

4.title: Tears, Envy and the Threefold Cord

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Tears with No One to Comfort
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher sees the oppressions done under the sun: the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them! Power is on the side of the oppressors (v. 1). He calls the dead more fortunate than the living (v. 2), and the one never born better than both, because he has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Under the sun, the oppressed have no comforter; the God of all comfort is the answer the chapter longs for.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them! On the side of their oppressors there was power, and there was no one to comfort them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tears of the oppressed. In chapter 3 he held on to the truth that God will judge. But judgment is future, and the tears are now, so he looks again and sees the faces: the worker cheated of wages, the widow whose land was taken, the prisoner beaten.

No one to comfort. He says it twice, and the repetition is a cry. Lamentations has the same grief: my eyes flow with tears; for a comforter is far from me (Lam 1:16).

The Bible does not look away, and Christians must not either. Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated (Heb 13:3). And the Bible answers the double cry with a double name: the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction (2 Cor 1:3-4). The one who was himself oppressed and stood silent before his accusers promised his followers another Helper, to be with you forever (John 14:16). No believer is left with no one to comfort him, and no believer should leave the oppressed with no one either.

verseByVerse.quote: And I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive. But better than both is he who has not yet been and has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is as dark as Scripture gets. Job said it too: Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire? (Job 3:11). So did Jeremiah: Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow (Jer 20:18).

God put these words in his book, and that is a kindness: people crushed by what they have seen need to know that the Bible has said it aloud. The Preacher is not recommending death. He is saying how heavy the weight of evil is when it is seen only from under the sun. If you have felt this, say it to God as honestly as these men did, and tell someone you trust; if you have begun to think of ending your life, seek help today, from a doctor, a pastor or an emergency line. Then keep reading. The book does not stop here, and neither does God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — Envy, Idleness and the Lonely Miser
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Much toil is driven by a man's envy of his neighbor (v. 4). The fool who does nothing destroys himself (v. 5), yet Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind (v. 6). And there is the man alone, with no son or brother, working endlessly and never asking, For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure? (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Work driven by envy or greed empties the worker; a quiet handful is richer than two restless fists.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From oppression to a sickness within. Why do people work so hard? Much of it, the Preacher says, is envy: the bigger house next door, the colleague's promotion. We call it ambition. He calls it envy, and breath.

Not all work is envious. But ask honestly how much of your effort would continue if no one else could see the result. A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot (Prov 14:30). The gospel frees a person from that race, because his worth is settled in Christ, and so he can work for others rather than against them: Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others (Phil 2:4).

verseByVerse.quote: The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh. Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fool folds his hands. Idleness is not the answer either: the fool starves himself by doing nothing. A little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber (Prov 6:10-11).

A handful of quietness. The wise middle. Picture three pairs of hands: the fool's folded, the envious worker's both full and clutching, and the wise person's one hand full and at peace.

Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it (Prov 15:16). Many people are already paying for their income with their peace. Jesus offers what the overfilled hands cannot hold: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Again, I saw vanity under the sun: one person who has no other, either son or brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches, so that he never asks, "For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?" This also is vanity and an unhappy business.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One alone. A new portrait: the man with no one to share with or leave anything to, who works without end. His eyes, like those of 1:8, are never satisfied. He cannot stop. The Preacher is not faulting anyone for being single or childless. The vanity is the endless grasping that has no one to share it with and no reason to stop.

For whom? The tragedy is also the question he never asks. He deprives himself of every pleasure to pile up money for no one he loves. The rich fool in Jesus' parable heard the same question from God: the things you have prepared, whose will they be? (Luke 12:20).

Ask it of your own week. For whom are you working? If the honest answer is "no one, really", something has gone wrong that more money will not fix.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — Two Are Better Than One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two are better than one: they share the reward (v. 9), lift each other when one falls (v. 10), keep each other warm (v. 11), and stand together against an attacker, for a threefold cord is not quickly broken (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: God did not make people to live alone, and the answer to the lonely miser is companionship.

verseByVerse.quote: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two are better than one. Against the lonely miser, companionship. Being alone is the first thing in all creation that God called not good: It is not good that the man should be alone (Gen 2:18).

If they fall. Everyone falls: into sin, sickness, grief, a ditch on a dark road. The question is whether anyone will be close enough to reach you when you do.

This is one reason God puts believers in churches. Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ (Gal 6:2). Who would lift you up if you fell tomorrow? And whom are you close enough to lift?

verseByVerse.quote: Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone? And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him—a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone? A traveller's picture: a cold night on the road, and two people sharing warmth. It applies to marriage, but not only to marriage. Friendship, fellowship and family all keep a person warm in a cold world.

A threefold cord. A robber can overpower one traveller; two stand him off, and three strands twisted together hold what none could hold alone.

The verse is often read at weddings, with Christ as the third strand between husband and wife. The Preacher first meant companions in general, but it is a true application. A marriage, or a friendship, bound together with Christ holds in the storm. Let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together (Heb 10:24-25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — The Wise Youth and the Fickle Crowd
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Better was a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knew how to take advice (v. 13). The youth rises from prison to the throne (v. 14), and all the people follow him (vv. 15-16). Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Popularity is breath. The crowd that crowns a king today will forget him tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Better was a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knew how to take advice. For he went from prison to the throne, though in his own kingdom he had been born poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The old king. Now a short story. An old king has become a man who cannot be told anything; age and power often destroy teachability.

Prison to the throne. The youth rises from nothing to the crown. The Bible has such stories: Joseph was brought quickly out of the pit to stand before Pharaoh (Gen 41:14), and David was a shepherd boy before he was king.

verseByVerse.quote: I saw all the living who move about under the sun, along with that youth who was to stand in the king's place. There was no end of all the people, all of whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd. Everyone flocks to the new man; that youth is in Hebrew "the second", the successor (ESV note). And then the sting: the next generation will want their own new face.

Popularity is breath, as every leader learns. Jerusalem's crowds shouted Hosanna to Jesus as he rode in, and within the week a crowd was shouting for his death. He never entrusted himself to the crowd's applause (John 2:24), and his kingdom does not depend on the crowd's favour. The Preacher's youth is not a picture of Christ, but the contrast is plain: every king who rises is replaced by the next, and the King who rose from the grave to the throne has no successor. Of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:33).

4.overview:
The Preacher sees the tears of the oppressed, with power on the side of the oppressors and no one to comfort them (v. 1). He calls the dead more fortunate than the living, and the unborn better still (vv. 2-3).

Much toil comes from envy, idleness destroys the fool, and a handful of quietness is better (vv. 4-6). The lonely man works without end (vv. 7-8), but Two are better than one (vv. 9-12). Even the youth who rises to the throne is forgotten (vv. 13-16).
4.theology:
Scripture looks honestly at oppression and at the despair it produces (vv. 1-3; Job 3:11; Jer 20:18). The answer to the cry for a comforter is the God of all comfort (2 Cor 1:3-4) and the Helper Christ promised (John 14:16), and his people are to comfort the oppressed (Heb 13:3).

Envy corrupts work, and idleness destroys the idle; contentment with quietness is better (vv. 4-6; Prov 15:16). God made people for companionship (vv. 9-12; Gen 2:18) and gives the church to bear one another's burdens (Gal 6:2). Human popularity is fleeting (vv. 13-16); only Christ's reign has no end.
4.examples:
Working harder because of the neighbour's bigger house.

Three pairs of hands: folded, clutching, and one handful at rest.

The man with no heirs who cannot stop working.

Falling on a dark road with no one near enough to help.

Hosanna on Sunday and "Crucify" on Friday.

5.title: Guard Your Steps: Worship, Vows and the Love of Money

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Guard Your Steps in the House of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. Listening is better than the sacrifice of fools (v. 1). God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few (vv. 2-3). Pay what you vow, and do not call it a mistake afterward (vv. 4-6). Many words are vanity, but God is the one you must fear (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: True worship begins with listening to God, and reverence shows itself in few, honest words.

verseByVerse.quote: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Guard your steps. After four chapters of observing, the Preacher speaks in commands, and the first place he sends us is the house of God. If life is breath, how should a person approach the God above it all? Carefully.

Draw near to listen. The fool comes to worship to do something: say his piece, tick the box. The wise person comes to listen. Samuel told Saul the same thing: to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams (1 Sam 15:22). The fool thinks religious activity pleases God regardless of his heart. This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me (Matt 15:8).

What do you come to church to do? The verse says the first thing is to hear. Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak (Jas 1:19).
verseByVerse.note: Ecclesiastes 5:1 is 4:17 in the Hebrew numbering (ESV note at 5:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few. For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is in heaven. Here is the reason for reverence: the distance between Creator and creature is infinite. Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases (Ps 115:3). So the fitting response is few words, carefully meant.

Jesus taught the same: when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words (Matt 6:7). And then he taught his disciples a prayer that begins, "Our Father in heaven". He is in heaven, so we come with awe. He is our Father, so we come without fear, and his Spirit helps us when we do not know what to pray. In Christ we may with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:16), and still offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire (Heb 12:28-29). Confidence without reverence becomes chatter. Reverence without confidence becomes dread.

A dream comes. A busy mind produces restless dreams, and a fool a stream of talk, in prayer as much as anywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow. It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay. Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay what you vow. A vow was a voluntary promise to God, often made in a moment of need. The law said the same: If you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it and if you refrain from vowing, you will not be guilty of sin (Deut 23:21-22). A promise to God is not a mood but a debt. Think of the promises made in hospital waiting rooms and forgotten when the danger passed.

It is a snare to say rashly, "It is holy," and to reflect only after making vows (Prov 20:25). Jephthah made a rash vow and lived to say, I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow (Judg 11:35). Ananias and Sapphira pretended to give everything and kept part back, and Peter said, You have not lied to man but to God (Acts 5:4).

Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands? The ESV notes that your mouth is in Hebrew "your flesh", and that messenger may be rendered "angel". The picture is of a person going back on his promise before God's representative and excusing it as an honest mistake. God is not fooled.

Christians make vows too: at baptism, marriage, membership, ordination. Jesus' rule covers all our words: Let what you say be simply 'Yes' or 'No' (Matt 5:37). Is there a promise you made to God that you have quietly reclassified as a mistake? Then do not hide it; confess it and, where you still can, keep it. Every promise God has made finds its Yes in Christ (2 Cor 1:20), the one man who kept every vow, and If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9).
verseByVerse.note: “The messenger” may be rendered “angel” (ESV note); probably the priest or temple official.

verseByVerse.quote: For when dreams increase and words grow many, there is vanity; but God is the one you must fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dreams and many words are breath (the ESV note offers another rendering, "For when dreams and vanities increase, words also grow many"). Religious talk, spiritual feelings and elaborate promises can all be vapour.

What is solid? God is the one you must fear. This is the second time the book has named the fear of God (3:14), and it stands here as the centre of true worship. It is not a feeling to work up, but a settled seriousness about who God is. A person who fears God will say less to him and mean more of it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oppression in a province should not amaze anyone, for officials watch officials, all the way up (vv. 8-9). He who loves money will not be satisfied with money (v. 10). More goods bring more eaters (v. 11), and Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, while the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Money promises satisfaction and security; it delivers neither.

verseByVerse.quote: If you see in a province the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness, do not be amazed at the matter, for the high official is watched by a higher, and there are yet higher ones over them. But this is gain for a land in every way: a king committed to cultivated fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be amazed. From the house of God to the halls of government. The Preacher is a realist: layers of officials watch one another, each protecting his position and taking his cut.

But read the ladder to the top. Above the highest official there is one higher still. God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment (Ps 82:1). No official is finally unaccountable. There is no authority except from God (Rom 13:1), and every authority will answer to him.

Gain for a land. The Hebrew here is uncertain (ESV note), so hold it lightly. As the ESV renders it, against the self-serving officials stands a king whose concern is the fields that feed the people.

verseByVerse.quote: He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income; this also is vanity. When goods increase, they increase who eat them, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who loves money. Few sentences have been proved true more often. Money promises that the next level will be enough, and when you reach it, it has moved.

Money is not the problem. The love of it is. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Tim 6:10). The cure is not poverty but contentment rooted in God's presence: Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, "I will never leave you nor forsake you" (Heb 13:5).

When goods increase, they increase who eat them, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes? More income brings more mouths: staff, advisers, tax, maintenance, relatives, and a bigger house to heat. The owner's only advantage is looking at what he has. The larger the estate, the more of it is consumed by others. One's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep.
verseByVerse.commentary: The rich man lies awake, his stomach and his mind both overloaded. Sleep is one thing money cannot buy. The psalmist found the secret of it in God: You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Ps 4:7-8). Where does your mind go when you cannot sleep? It often shows where your treasure is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Riches Lost, and Naked We Go
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Riches hoarded to the owner's hurt are lost in a bad venture, and he has nothing to leave his son (vv. 13-14). As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came (v. 15). He toiled for the wind, and ate all his days in darkness and vexation (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Everyone leaves the world with empty hands; the only question is what he lived for.

verseByVerse.quote: There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches were kept by their owner to his hurt, and those riches were lost in a bad venture. And he is father of a son, but he has nothing in his hand. As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry away in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A grievous evil. A story everyone has seen: wealth hoarded, then gone in one bad venture, and a son with nothing to receive.

Naked as he came. Even if the venture had succeeded, the end would be the same. Job said it as he lost everything: Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return (Job 1:21). Paul said it to Timothy: we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world (1 Tim 6:7). There are no pockets in a shroud.

But Jesus showed a way to send treasure ahead: Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail (Luke 12:33).

verseByVerse.quote: This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind? Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind? The question of 1:3 again, and a new picture: toils for the wind. A lifetime of work, and the wages paid in wind. That is what it is to work only for what we can keep.

Eats in darkness. The hoarder did not even enjoy the journey. The love of money failed to give him a future, and it took his present. Paul says that some who craved money have pierced themselves with many pangs (1 Tim 6:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What is good and fitting is to eat, drink and enjoy one's toil in the few days God gives (v. 18). The power to enjoy wealth and accept one's lot is the gift of God (v. 19), and God keeps such a person occupied with joy in his heart (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The ability to enjoy what we have is itself God's gift, and it frees us from the anxious counting of days.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot. Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil—this is the gift of God. For he will not much remember the days of his life because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold. After the dark portrait, the "nothing better" passage returns (2:24; 3:12-13, 22): look at this instead. Find enjoyment may be rendered "see good" (ESV note). The hoarder ate in darkness; the one who receives life from God sees the good.

The gift of God. There are three gifts here. Wealth is a gift. The power to enjoy it is a second, separate gift, and chapter 6 will show a man who had the first without the second. And the ability to accept his lot, to be content with the portion God has given, is a third. Godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Tim 6:6). The rich are to set their hope on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy, and to be generous and ready to share (1 Tim 6:17-18).

Occupied with joy. The person who receives life as God's gift is not forever counting his days. Like a child absorbed in play who forgets the clock, he is too busy enjoying God's gifts to be consumed by fear of losing them. It is God's gift, not a technique.
