5.overview: The Preacher turns to worship: listen, let your words be few, pay what you vow, and fear God (vv. 1-7). Officials watch officials (vv. 8-9); the love of money never satisfies, and everyone leaves as naked as he came (vv. 10-17). The power to enjoy what one has is the gift of God (vv. 18-20).
5.theology:
Worship begins with listening and reverent fear, not many words (vv. 1-7; 1 Sam 15:22; Matt 6:7). God is in heaven, and in Christ believers may draw near with confidence and with reverence (Heb 4:16; 12:28-29). Promises to God are binding (vv. 4-6; Deut 23:21-23; Matt 5:37).

All earthly authority is accountable to a higher, and finally to God (vv. 8-9; Ps 82:1). The love of money cannot be satisfied and brings misery (vv. 10-17; 1 Tim 6:6-10); everyone leaves the world with nothing (v. 15; Job 1:21). Wealth, the power to enjoy it and contentment with one's lot are separate gifts of God (vv. 18-20; 1 Tim 6:17).
5.examples:
Coming to church to say your piece rather than to hear.

Promises made in hospital waiting rooms.

The lottery winner for whom enough keeps moving.

The labourer asleep and the rich man lying awake.

There are no pockets in a shroud.

A child too absorbed in play to watch the clock.

6.title: Wealth Without Enjoyment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Wealth Without the Power to Enjoy It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A grievous evil: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, and a stranger enjoys them (vv. 1-2). A man with a hundred children and many years, unsatisfied and unburied, is worse off than a stillborn child (vv. 3-5). Even two thousand years without good end in the one place (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Having everything is not the same as enjoying anything; enjoyment is a separate gift of God.

verseByVerse.quote: There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heavy on mankind. Chapter 5 ended with the gift of joy; chapter 6 shows its absence, and it is not rare.

No power to enjoy. The man has everything and lacks nothing. Put this beside 5:19: wealth and enjoyment are two different gifts, and God can give the first and withhold the second.

Many people pray for the first gift and never ask for the second. The capacity to be happy in the house, the job or the money is not included in the purchase. It comes from God. Why would God withhold it? The Preacher does not say. But Scripture shows that gifts loved apart from the Giver cannot satisfy, and the restlessness they leave can be a mercy that drives a person to God himself. The man who has it all without that capacity watches a stranger enjoy what he worked for. Ask God for what you want if you must. Ask him first for a heart that can receive with joy what he has already given.

verseByVerse.quote: If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he. For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered. Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A hundred children. Many children and long life were Israel's highest blessings, and this man has both in exaggerated measure. But his soul is unsatisfied, and he is not even buried with honour. Scripture treats an unburied body as disgrace; Jeremiah said of a faithless king, With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried (Jer 22:19). The verdict is shocking: a stillborn child is better off than he.

It finds rest. The stillborn child never saw the light or had a name spoken, yet it finds rest. The rich man never did.

Parents who have lost a child before birth may find these verses hard to read, and they deserve a word. The Preacher is not saying the child's life did not matter. He is saying, from under the sun, that even the shortest life is not the worst fate. The worst fate is a long life with a restless soul. And the God who knows the name that was never spoken aloud has not lost that child.

verseByVerse.quote: Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good—do not all go to the one place?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Double the longest life in Scripture, and more. Without good ("see" no good, ESV note), what has length added? Nothing, because all go to the one place (3:20).

A long life without joy is only a long walk to the same grave; a short life lived with God is full. We spend fortunes adding years to life; have we thought as hard about adding life to our years?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Who Knows What Is Good for Man?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied (v. 7). The wise and the poor have no final advantage (v. 8); what is in front of the eyes is better than wandering desire (v. 9). Man cannot dispute with one stronger than he, and more words only add vanity (vv. 10-11). For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The book's first half ends with a question only God can answer.

verseByVerse.quote: All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied. For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living? Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For his mouth. We work to eat, and we are hungry again. Satisfied is in Hebrew "filled" (ESV note): the appetite is a vessel with a hole in the bottom, and the soul's deeper appetite is never filled by what we work for. Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? (Isa 55:2).

Jesus spoke to exactly this: Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you (John 6:27).

For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living? The wise man's appetite is as unfilled as the fool's. The poor man who has learned good manners and good sense still goes hungry. Under the sun, wisdom and decency do not fill the hole.

The sight of the eyes. Practical wisdom, if not a final answer: be content with what is in front of you, the meal on the table rather than the one in the advertisement. Yet even that contentment, on its own, is breath. It helps; it does not save.

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he. The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already named. To name something is often to know it and have authority over it. God determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names (Ps 147:4). Everything has already been named by God, and it is known what man is: a creature of dust. So man cannot take God to court and win. Isaiah said, Woe to him who strives with him who formed him (Isa 45:9), and Paul, But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? (Rom 9:20).

The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man? Arguments with God multiply words, and words multiply breath. This echoes 5:2-3. When we cannot understand God, the answer is not more talk, but trust. Job came to the same place: after all his speeches, he laid his hand on his mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first half of Ecclesiastes ends with two questions, and they are the right questions. What is good for us, in our short, breath-like life? The ESV's note marks vain as hebel again: a breath of a life. And what will happen after we are gone?

Life passes like a shadow. David prayed, Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding (1 Chr 29:15). Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow (Ps 144:4).

From under the sun, no one can answer them. Chapters 7-12 offer wisdom for how to live, but the final answer to "who knows what is good for man?" must come from above. And it has. He has told you, O man, what is good (Mic 6:8). And it has come in a person, who said, I came that they may have life and have it abundantly (John 10:10). The shadow is not the end for those who belong to him, because he is the light.

For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?
6.overview: A man has wealth and honour from God but not the power to enjoy them, and is worse off than a stillborn child (vv. 1-6). The appetite is never filled, and man cannot dispute with his Maker (vv. 7-11). The chapter ends with two questions: who knows what is good for man, and what will come after him? (v. 12).
6.theology:
Wealth and the power to enjoy it are separate gifts of God; he may give one and withhold the other (v. 2; 5:19). Neither long life nor many children can satisfy the soul (vv. 3-6). Human appetite is never filled by what it works for (v. 7; Isa 55:2), but Christ gives food that endures to eternal life (John 6:27).

God has named and defined all things, and man cannot contend with his Maker (v. 10; Isa 45:9; Rom 9:20). Life is a shadow (v. 12; Ps 144:4), and what is good for man is revealed by God, not discovered under the sun (Mic 6:8; John 10:10).
6.examples:
Praying for the house and never for a heart to enjoy it.

A hundred children and no mourners.

Adding years to life, and forgetting to add life to the years.

An appetite like a vessel with a hole in the bottom.

The meal on the table rather than the one in the advertisement.

7.title: Better Things: Mourning, Patience and the Upright Made Crooked

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth (v. 1). The house of mourning teaches more than the house of feasting (vv. 2-4), and a wise rebuke more than a fool's song (vv. 5-7). Patience is better than pride and anger, and nostalgia is not wisdom (vv. 8-10). Wisdom protects like money (vv. 11-12). Consider the work of God: In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider, for God made both (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The things that humble and sober us are often better for the soul than the things that please us.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first half ended by asking who knows what is good for man? (6:12). Chapter 7 begins to answer with "better" sayings, and the first are startling. Perfume fades; a good name lasts. A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches (Prov 22:1). Then the shock: the day of death than the day of birth. At a birth nothing is settled; at a death the life is complete and its name is known.

For the believer the day of death is the day of going home. Paul could say, For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain, and My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Phil 1:21, 23). The Preacher saw that death finishes a life; the gospel shows that for those in Christ it begins a better one.
verseByVerse.note: A sound-play: a good name (shem) is better than precious ointment (shemen).

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart. Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad. The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house of mourning. Which invitation would you rather accept this weekend, the party or the funeral? Almost everyone chooses the party. The Preacher says the funeral is better for you. At the party you forget that you will die. At the funeral you remember, and the living will lay it to heart.

That is not morbid. A person who has stood at a graveside and let it sink in makes different decisions on Monday.

Sorrow is better than laughter. A paradox: the sorrow that faces reality honestly does a deep work that laughter cannot. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret (2 Cor 7:10). And Jesus said, Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:4). The gladness on the other side of mourning is deeper than the gladness that avoids it.

The heart of the wise. Where does your heart go when it is free to go anywhere? The fool's heart runs to entertainment, always, to avoid thinking. The wise heart is willing to sit with grief, its own and others'. Our culture has built a house of mirth that never closes, a screen in every pocket. Ask what it is helping you not to feel.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better for a man to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools. For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fools; this also is vanity. Surely oppression drives the wise into madness, and a bribe corrupts the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebuke. The wise friend who tells you the truth does more good than a room full of people telling you what you want to hear. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Prov 27:6). David prayed for such wounds: let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head (Ps 141:5). Who in your life is allowed to tell you that you are wrong?

Thorns under a pot. A quick, loud blaze, gone before the pot boils: so is the fool's laughter.

Oppression and bribes. Even the wise man is not immune: long pressure can drive him to folly, and a bribe can bend his heart. For a bribe blinds the clear-sighted (Exod 23:8). Wisdom must be guarded, not assumed.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is the end of a thing than its beginning, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools. Say not, "Why were the former days better than these?" For it is not from wisdom that you ask this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better is the end. Anyone can start a marriage, a project, a Christian life; the end tells the truth. What gets a person there is patience, not pride: the proud want the result now and quit when it does not come.

Anger lodges. Anger nursed and held close ("in the bosom", see the note) settles in and makes a home. It may flash in a wise person; it lodges in a fool. Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger (Eph 4:26), for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God (Jas 1:20).

The former days. Nostalgia feels wise, and it is not. Israel in the wilderness remembered the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing (Num 11:5), and forgot the whips. The question is a way of refusing the present God has given. Paul's way is better: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead (Phil 3:13).
verseByVerse.note: “Lodges in the heart” is literally “in the bosom” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom is good with an inheritance, an advantage to those who see the sun. For the protection of wisdom is like the protection of money, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of him who has it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom with an inheritance. An inheritance without wisdom is soon wasted; with wisdom it becomes a blessing.

Protection. Money gives a kind of shelter, and so does wisdom, but wisdom preserves the life of its owner. Money can be lost in a bad venture (5:14); wisdom keeps a person from walking into the disasters that money cannot repair.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked? In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that man may not find out anything that will be after him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked? In 1:15 the Preacher said, What is crooked cannot be made straight. Here he says who bent it: God. Some things in your life God has made crooked: the illness, the child who was never born, the marriage that never came. You cannot straighten them, and you are not asked to. This does not mean God takes pleasure in your pain, or that it is a punishment for some hidden sin. You are asked to consider the work of God, to look at them as his work and not as random chaos.

That is hard. It is also a comfort, because what God has bent, God can straighten, and one day will. The uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain (Isa 40:4).

Prosperity and adversity. On a good day, rejoice; do not spoil it with worry. On a bad day, consider: remember who made this day. Both come from the same hand. Job said, Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? (Job 2:10). Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that good and bad come? (Lam 3:38).

God mixes them so that we cannot predict our lives or trust in our predictions. We are left to trust God, who for those who love God makes all things work together for good (Rom 8:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — The Fear of God Between Two Ditches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The righteous sometimes perish and the wicked live long (v. 15). Be not overly righteous, Be not overly wicked, for the one who fears God shall come out from both of them (vv. 16-18). Wisdom strengthens, yet there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins (vv. 19-20), so do not take to heart every word said against you (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of God keeps a person from both self-righteousness and licence, and the knowledge of his own sin keeps him gentle.

verseByVerse.quote: In my vain life I have seen everything. There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evildoing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher faces what Proverbs, taken as a set of guarantees, cannot explain. A righteous man dies young in his righteousness, while he is living it. A wicked man lives to ninety.

Scripture does not hide it. The righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart (Isa 57:1). Jesus was asked about people who died in a disaster and said, do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others? (Luke 13:4). Suffering in this life is not a precise measure of sin, and this life cannot be the whole of justice. The clearest case of all is the cross: the one truly righteous man perished in his righteousness, while the guilty went free, and on the third day God showed that his story did not end there (Acts 2:23-24). Because he lives, the righteous who perish young are not lost.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself? Be not overly wicked, neither be a fool. Why should you die before your time? It is good that you should take hold of this, and from that withhold not your hand, for the one who fears God shall come out from both of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself? This verse is often misread as "don't be too religious". It cannot mean that; Scripture never warns against too much real holiness. The warning is against a self-made righteousness, a performance of goodness that tries to force God's hand and guarantee a good life. Seeing in verse 15 that the righteous sometimes perish, a person might try harder, stricter, more rules, more display, as if he could buy immunity. The Pharisee in the temple prayed, God, I thank you that I am not like other men (Luke 18:11). That road destroys a person: it breeds pride, exhaustion and harshness, and it never reaches God.

Be not overly wicked, neither be a fool. Why should you die before your time? The opposite ditch. Having seen the wicked live long, a person might decide that goodness does not pay and throw himself into evil. That road also kills. Folly brings its own early grave.

The one who fears God. The way between the ditches is not moderation, a little goodness and a little sin. The fear of God frees a person from both performance and rebellion. He does not try to earn God's favour, which is given, and he does not despise it. He trusts God, obeys him in the strength of the Spirit God gives his people (Ezek 36:27; Gal 5:16), and leaves the outcome to God. That is the only road that comes out safely from both of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom gives strength to the wise man more than ten rulers who are in a city. Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten rulers. Wisdom is a stronger defence than a council of the powerful.

Not a righteous man. And yet even the wise man sins. This is one of the clearest Old Testament statements of universal sinfulness. Solomon prayed at the temple dedication, for there is no one who does not sin (1 Kgs 8:46). Paul gathered the Old Testament's witness: None is righteous, no, not one (Rom 3:10). If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8).

It is also why verse 16 matters: no one can be righteous enough to guarantee anything. The only hope is mercy. There has been one righteous man who did good and never sinned, and by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous (Rom 5:19). His obedience is counted to all who trust him, and so failure is not the end: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not take to heart all the things that people say, lest you hear your servant cursing you. Your heart knows that many times you yourself have cursed others.
verseByVerse.commentary: A practical application of verse 20. People will say things about you. Go listening for every word and you will hear something cruel, even from someone who works for you. And before you get indignant, remember your own mouth: your heart knows. Knowing your own sin makes you slower to be crushed by other people's words, and slower to condemn them. Judge not, that you be not judged (Matt 7:1). Grace received makes a thick skin and a soft heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — Searching for Wisdom, Finding Sin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher tried to be wise, but wisdom was far off, and deep, very deep (vv. 23-24). Searching out folly, he found the seductress more bitter than death (vv. 25-26). Adding one thing to another, he found few upright (vv. 27-28). See, this alone I found, that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The deepest thing the search uncovers is the fall: God made us upright, and we made ourselves crooked.

verseByVerse.quote: All this I have tested by wisdom. I said, "I will be wise," but it was far from me. That which has been is far off, and deep, very deep; who can find it out?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far from me. A confession from the wisest man in Jerusalem: the more he learned, the further off the full answer seemed.

That which has been is far off, and deep, very deep; who can find it out? Reality itself is deep, very deep. Job asked, But where shall wisdom be found? and answered, it is not found in the land of the living (Job 28:12-13). Paul, at the end of his greatest argument, could only worship: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments (Rom 11:33). The right response to a depth you cannot plumb is not despair, but humility.

verseByVerse.quote: I turned my heart to know and to search out and to seek wisdom and the scheme of things, and to know the wickedness of folly and the foolishness that is madness. And I find something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scheme of things. Once more he gives himself to the search, and the first thing he finds is a trap. This is the seductress Proverbs warns against: For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood (Prov 5:3-4); Her house is the way to Sheol (Prov 7:27). Sexual sin promises sweetness and delivers bondage: snares and nets, fetters. Many men have found it more bitter than death, because it destroyed the marriage, the family and the name that death would have left intact.

The escape is not cleverness but God: the one who walks with God is kept.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, this is what I found, says the Preacher, while adding one thing to another to find the scheme of things— which my soul has sought repeatedly, but I have not found. One man among a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I have not found. See, this alone I found, that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One among a thousand. The frame narrator speaks again, says the Preacher, as in 1:2 and 12:8. Looking for the truly upright person, the Preacher found almost no one.

This is a hard verse, and it must be read carefully. It is not the Bible's verdict on women. The same wisdom literature says He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD (Prov 18:22), and celebrates the excellent wife as far more precious than jewels (Prov 31:10). The Preacher is reporting his own search in his own world, and his real point is how rare uprightness is at all: one in a thousand is almost none. The next verse makes clear that the problem he found is not one sex, but the whole race.

Upright, but many schemes. Here is the one sure thing his search uncovered: the doctrine of the fall in a sentence. Humanity, male and female, was created in God's image and called very good (Gen 1:27, 31). The Preacher searched for the scheme of things; what human beings have produced is many schemes for getting around God.

The world is not crooked because God made it badly. It is crooked because we bent it. Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin (Rom 5:12). That is humbling, and it is also hopeful. What was made upright can be made upright again, and in Christ it is: you are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal 3:28), men and women alike, forgiven and renewed.

I said, "I will be wise," but it was far from me.<sup>24</sup>That which has been is far off, and deep, very deep; who can find it out?<sup>25</sup>I turned my heart to know and to search out and to seek wisdom and the scheme of things, and to know the wickedness of folly and the foolishness that is madness.<sup>26</sup>And I find something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her.<sup>27</sup>Behold, this is what I found, says the Preacher, while adding one thing to another to find the scheme of things—<sup>28</sup>which my soul has sought repeatedly, but I have not found. One man among a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I have not found.<sup>29</sup>See, this alone I found, that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes.
7.overview:
The chapter begins to answer the question of 6:12 with "better" sayings: mourning, rebuke and patience teach more than feasting and pride, and God makes both prosperity and adversity (vv. 1-14).

The righteous sometimes perish; the one who fears God escapes both self-made righteousness and wickedness, and no one on earth never sins (vv. 15-22).

Wisdom is very deep, and the Preacher's one certain discovery is the fall: God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes (vv. 23-29).
7.theology:
Facing death and sorrow honestly produces wisdom (vv. 1-4; Ps 90:12; Matt 5:4); for believers, death is gain (Phil 1:21). God sovereignly ordains both prosperity and adversity (vv. 13-14; Lam 3:38) and works all things for good for those who love him (Rom 8:28).

The fear of God delivers from both self-righteousness and licence (vv. 16-18; Luke 18:11). All people sin (v. 20; 1 Kgs 8:46; Rom 3:10), and the only hope is God's forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

God created humanity upright, and humanity fell by its own schemes (v. 29; Gen 1:27, 31; Rom 5:12). The problem of sin belongs to men and women alike, and so does the remedy in Christ (Gal 3:28).
7.examples:
Choosing between the party and the funeral this weekend.

The friend who is allowed to tell you that you are wrong.

Thorns crackling under a pot.

Remembering the fish in Egypt and forgetting the whips.

The Pharisee's prayer, and the ditch on the other side of the road.

Listening for every word said about you.

8.title: The King's Word and the Delay of Justice

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Wise Man Before the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom makes a man's face shine (v. 1). Keep the king's command, do not rush from his presence or stand in an evil cause, for his word is supreme (vv. 2-4). The wise heart knows the proper time and the just way, though no one knows the future (vv. 5-7). No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death (v. 8), and the Preacher has seen man rule over man to his hurt (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Earthly rulers deserve wise submission, but every ruler stands powerless before death and before God.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is like the wise? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.
verseByVerse.commentary: Wisdom shows on the face: the hard, set expression of anxiety or pride is softened, as in faces made gentle by years of walking wisely with God. Moses came down from meeting God with his face shining. Paul says that something like it is happening to every believer: we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image (2 Cor 3:18). The wisdom that changes the face is finally the wisdom of knowing Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I say: Keep the king's command, because of God's oath to him. Be not hasty to go from his presence. Do not take your stand in an evil cause, for he does whatever he pleases. For the word of the king is supreme, and who may say to him, "What are you doing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep the king's command. I say is not in the Hebrew, and the second half may be rendered "because of your oath to God" (ESV note). Either way, obedience to the king is tied to God: civil obedience is a religious matter.

The New Testament says the same: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God (Rom 13:1), and Fear God. Honor the emperor (1 Pet 2:17). A Christian is to be a good citizen, not because rulers are always good, but because God ordains authority.

Be not hasty. A courtier's wisdom: do not storm out of the king's presence or join a rebellion; resisting rashly gets people killed.

But there is a limit, and Scripture marks it. When a king commands what God forbids, the answer is Peter's: We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego honoured Nebuchadnezzar and refused his idol: But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods (Dan 3:18).

Then the question who may say to him, "What are you doing?" It is true of an earthly king only for a while. It is true of God forever. Nebuchadnezzar himself learned to say of God, none can stay his hand or say to him, "What have you done?" (Dan 4:35).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps a command will know no evil thing, and the wise heart will know the proper time and the just way. For there is a time and a way for everything, although man's trouble lies heavy on him. For he does not know what is to be, for who can tell him how it will be?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proper time and the just way. Wisdom knows not only what to do, but when and how (the just way may be rendered "judgment", ESV note). The right words at the wrong moment can be as foolish as the wrong words.

For there is a time and a way for everything, although man's trouble lies heavy on him. For he does not know what is to be, for who can tell him how it will be? This echoes chapter 3: a time and a way for everything. But now with a weight added. The ESV notes that trouble may be rendered "evil". Knowing that there is a right time does not mean we know when it is. He does not know what is to be. That uncertainty presses on every decision.

James draws the Christian conclusion: you do not know what tomorrow will bring, so you ought to say, "If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that" (Jas 4:14-15). Uncertainty is meant to drive us to dependence.

verseByVerse.quote: No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death. There is no discharge from war, nor will wickedness deliver those who are given to it. All this I observed while applying my heart to all that is done under the sun, when man had power over man to his hurt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No man has power. The king has great power, but not this: no one can hold on to his breath or move the day of his death. You have appointed his limits that he cannot pass (Job 14:5). Death is a war with no discharge, and wickedness cannot win it. The tyrant dies like the slave.

Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life (Ps 49:7). Only one man ever had power over the day of his death. Jesus said of his life, I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again (John 10:18). He entered the war that has no discharge and won it, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb 2:14).

Man over man. Power in human hands tends toward harm. That is why the powerless need a King above all kings.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — When the Sentence Is Delayed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wicked are buried with honour (v. 10). Because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed speedily, the heart of the children of man is fully set to do evil (v. 11). Yet it will be well with those who fear God and not with the wicked (vv. 12-13), though on earth the righteous and wicked sometimes receive each other's due (v. 14). And I commend joy (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's patience is not his indifference; judgment delayed is not judgment denied.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw the wicked buried. They used to go in and out of the holy place and were praised in the city where they had done such things. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary: A funeral with honours for a man who had been a regular at worship, praised by the city that watched him do his evil. Every generation has seen the eulogy that bore no resemblance to the life. Most Hebrew manuscripts read "forgotten" for praised (ESV note); either way, their end is breath. Jesus spoke of religious men who were like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones (Matt 23:27). The city's praise does not settle anything. God's verdict does.

verseByVerse.quote: Because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed speedily, the heart of the children of man is fully set to do evil.
verseByVerse.commentary: One of the sharpest observations in the book. When punishment is slow, people conclude it is not coming: the child never corrected, the fraud unnoticed for years, each learns to go further. So with God: because judgment has not fallen, they assume it never will. But Scripture reads the delay the other way: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Pet 3:9). The delay is mercy. To use it as permission is to be storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath (Rom 2:5). Is there a sin you continue in because nothing has happened yet? The patience is meant for you: turn now, and the mercy is there.

verseByVerse.quote: Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God, because they fear before him. But it will not be well with the wicked, neither will he prolong his days like a shadow, because he does not fear before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet I know. Now the Preacher speaks as a believer. He does not deny that the sinner lives long. Yet against all appearances, it will be well with those who fear God. This is not observation from under the sun. It is faith in what God has said. Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them (Isa 3:10).

Like a shadow. The wicked man's long days lengthen like an evening shadow just before it vanishes. The dividing line is fear before God, not wealth or reputation. Fret not yourself because of evildoers, For they will soon fade like the grass (Ps 37:1-2).

verseByVerse.quote: There is a vanity that takes place on earth, that there are righteous people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the wicked, and there are wicked people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Preacher does not let faith become a slogan that ignores the facts: the good man's business fails, and the crook's thrives. Both are true at once: verses 12-13 speak of the end, verse 14 of the meantime. Malachi heard people say, It is vain to serve God, Evildoers not only prosper but they put God to the test and they escape, and God answered, Then once more you shall see the distinction between the righteous and the wicked (Mal 3:14-15, 18). Abraham said to the rich man, you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here (Luke 16:25). The meantime is not the end.

verseByVerse.quote: And I commend joy, for man has nothing better under the sun but to eat and drink and be joyful, for this will go with him in his toil through the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After injustice, joy again. This is the fourth time the phrase nothing better appears in the book (2:24; 3:12, 22). It is not a shrug. It is a deliberate choice made in the face of everything he has just described. Precisely because the world is unjust and we cannot fix it or understand it, the Preacher "commends joy": receive God's daily gifts with gladness, and let that joy go with him in his toil.

Joy in a broken world is not denial. It is trust. The same God who will set everything right has given this meal, this work, this day. When Nehemiah's people wept over their sins, he told them to eat, drink and send portions to those who had nothing, for the joy of the LORD is your strength (Neh 8:10). Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice (Phil 4:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Work of God No One Can Find Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher gave his heart to know wisdom and watched the sleepless business of the earth (v. 16). Then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun; Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The limit of human wisdom is not a failure of effort; it is the boundary between creature and Creator.

verseByVerse.quote: When I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done on earth, how neither day nor night do one's eyes see sleep, then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out. Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither day nor night. The Preacher returns to his search, and to the sleepless busyness of the human race.

Cannot find it out. Three times in one verse. No effort will uncover the full meaning of God's work, and the wise man who claims to know is mistaken.

This is not anti-intellectual. It is honest about the size of God. Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! (Job 26:14). The humble response is Moses': The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law (Deut 29:29). You do not need to understand God's whole work to trust him and obey what he has revealed.

A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.<sup>2</sup>I say: Keep the king's command, because of God's oath to him.<sup>3</sup>Be not hasty to go from his presence. Do not take your stand in an evil cause, for he does whatever he pleases.<sup>4</sup>For the word of the king is supreme, and who may say to him, "What are you doing?"<sup>5</sup>Whoever keeps a command will know no evil thing, and the wise heart will know the proper time and the just way.<sup>6</sup>For there is a time and a way for everything, although man's trouble lies heavy on him.<sup>7</sup>For he does not know what is to be, for who can tell him how it will be?<sup>8</sup>No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death. I said that this also is vanity.<sup>15</sup>And I commend joy, for man has nothing better under the sun but to eat and drink and be joyful, for this will go with him in his toil through the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.<sup>16</sup>When I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done on earth, how neither day nor night do one's eyes see sleep,<sup>17</sup>then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out. Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out.
8.overview: The wise keep the king's command because of the oath before God, though no king has power over the day of death (vv. 1-9). Justice is delayed and the wicked are praised, yet it will be well with those who fear God, so the Preacher commends joy (vv. 10-15). No one can find out the whole work of God (vv. 16-17).
8.theology:
God ordains civil authority, and believers submit to it for his sake (vv. 2-4; Rom 13:1; 1 Pet 2:13-17), unless commanded to disobey God (Acts 5:29). No one has power over death (v. 8) except Christ, who laid down his life and took it up again (John 10:18; Heb 2:14).

God's delay in judgment is patience meant to lead to repentance, not indifference (v. 11; 2 Pet 3:9; Rom 2:4-5). It will be well with those who fear God (vv. 12-13), though the meantime is full of inversions (v. 14; Luke 16:25).

The full work of God cannot be found out by human wisdom (vv. 16-17; Job 26:14); what he has revealed is enough to live by (Deut 29:29).
8.examples:
A face made gentle by years of walking with God.

Storming out of the boss's office.

The eulogy that bore no resemblance to the life.

The fraud that goes unnoticed for years.

The shadow that lengthens just before it vanishes.

9.title: One Event for All, and Bread Eaten with Joy

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Same Event Happens to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The righteous and the wise are in the hand of God, though no one can read from events whether God's love or hate is on him (v. 1). It is the same for all: death comes to righteous and wicked alike, and the hearts of men are full of evil (vv. 2-3). A living dog is better than a dead lion (v. 4), for the dead have no more share in all that is done under the sun (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Circumstances cannot tell you whether God loves you; death comes to all; and life, while it lasts, is hope.

verseByVerse.quote: But all this I laid to heart, examining it all, how the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. Whether it is love or hate, man does not know; both are before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After confessing that no one can find out the work of God (8:17), the Preacher holds on to one thing: the righteous are in the hand of God. That is the believer's security when nothing else is clear. Jesus said of his sheep, no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand (John 10:29).

But he adds a hard truth: you cannot read God's heart toward you from your circumstances. A promotion is not proof of his favour; a diagnosis is not proof of his anger. Everything ahead is in his view, not ours.

So the believer does not look to his circumstances to learn whether God loves him. He looks to the cross, where God proved it.

verseByVerse.quote: It is the same for all, since the same event happens to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to him who sacrifices and him who does not sacrifice. As the good one is, so is the sinner, and he who swears is as he who shuns an oath. This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that the same event happens to all. Also, the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same event. Death, and six pairs prove that it comes to everyone: the hearse comes for the worshipper and the scoffer alike. (And the evil comes from ancient translations; the Hebrew lacks it, ESV note.)

This does not mean there is no difference between them. It means death does not show the difference. God makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good (Matt 5:45), and he lets the shadow of death fall on both. The difference will be shown on the other side.

Full of evil. Death is an evil, not natural or friendly. And he names a second evil, inside the heart, which is why death comes to all. The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick (Jer 17:9). Madness while we live, and then the grave. That is humanity without redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: But he who is joined with all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion. For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten. Their love and their hate and their envy have already perished, and forever they have no more share in all that is done under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A living dog. In Israel dogs were despised scavengers. David called himself a dead dog to show how low he was (1 Sam 24:14). Lions were the kings of beasts. Yet a living dog is better off than a dead lion, because while there is life, there is hope. The dog can still change.

This is a word to anyone who feels like the dog. While you are alive, it is not too late to repent and begin again with God. The thief on the cross had hours left, and they were enough.

The living know. The living know they will die, and can act on it.

Does this mean the dead are unconscious, or that the soul sleeps until the resurrection? Some sincere Christians have read it so, because they take these words at face value and because Scripture calls death a sleep (1 Thess 4:13). That word, though, describes how death looks from this side, and the certainty of waking. Read the last phrase: they have no more share in all that is done under the sun. The Preacher is speaking of the dead in relation to this world. They know nothing of what happens here, earn nothing here, love and hate nothing here. He is not describing what lies beyond, which the New Testament makes clear. Jesus told of a poor man who died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side, and a rich man who was fully conscious in Hades (Luke 16:22-23). Paul longed to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Phil 1:23). Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them! (Rev 14:13). Their share under the sun is over. Their life with God is not. So this commentary holds, with the Westminster Confession (32.1), that the souls of the righteous are received at death into the presence of God, while their bodies rest until the resurrection.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Go, Eat Your Bread with Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do (v. 7). Wear white and oil your head (v. 8). Enjoy life with the wife whom you love (v. 9). Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work in Sheol (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Life is short and death is certain, so receive each day's gifts gladly and work at each day's task wholeheartedly.

verseByVerse.quote: Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do. Let your garments be always white. Let not oil be lacking on your head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go, eat your bread with joy. Having looked death full in the face, the Preacher issues a command to enjoy. This is the fullest of the "nothing better" passages, and the shortness of life is a reason to take each meal as a gift.

And the ground of this joy is striking: God has already approved what you do. The person who fears God does not eat his supper wondering whether God is frowning at him for enjoying it. For the Christian this has a deeper root still. The believer does not work to win God's approval; he lives from it. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). You can enjoy your bread tonight because the verdict on you is already in.

White garments. White garments and oil were the clothes of a feast. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows (Ps 23:5). Live festively: not in excess, but in gladness. Many Christians have also heard an echo of the risen Christ's promise that his faithful people will walk with me in white (Rev 3:4), a feast begun in faith here that will go on forever.

Wine is God’s good gift, to be enjoyed with thanks (Ps 104:15), but never to drunkenness (Eph 5:18). Those who abstain for conscience or because they cannot drink safely are right to do so.

verseByVerse.quote: Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your vain life that he has given you under the sun, because that is your portion in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage is one of God's best gifts in a breath-like life. Life is short; do not waste it in coldness toward your spouse. Proverbs says the same: rejoice in the wife of your youth (Prov 5:18).

Your spouse is your portion, the share God has given you: not the fantasy someone else, but this person. Many marriages are poisoned by comparison. For Christians the pattern is set higher still, and it is a love first shown to us: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph 5:25).

When did you last simply enjoy your husband or wife, not as a partner in logistics, but as God's gift?

And if you are single or widowed? The verse does not say that a life without a spouse is no life. Each person's portion differs, and the same call holds for all: receive with joy the gifts God has given you, the friends, the work, the bread, and the Lord himself. Nor is the verse a call to endure abuse; anyone in danger at home should seek safety at once.

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joy in the gifts, and energy in the work: the task in front of you, not half-heartedly, not waiting for a more important job. The reason is the grave: in Sheol there is no work. Jesus said, We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work (John 9:4).

For the believer this is doubled. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men (Col 3:23). The dishes, the spreadsheet, the hospital shift: do it with your might, as service to Christ, who has already accepted you and gives his Spirit to strengthen the work.

Does this teach that the dead know nothing? Sheol here is the grave as seen from this world: the work of this life ends there. It does not deny conscious life after death, which Scripture teaches plainly for those in Christ (Phil 1:23; 2 Cor 5:8).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, but time and chance happen to them all (v. 11). Like fish in a net and birds in a snare, people are caught by an evil time that falls suddenly (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Ability does not guarantee outcomes; only God holds the times.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I saw that under the sun the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to those with knowledge, but time and chance happen to them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five things we expect, usually, perhaps, not always. The favourite stumbles; the brilliant graduate cannot find work.

From under the sun, it looks like chance. Scripture shows what lies behind it. The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov 16:33). The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD (Prov 21:31). What looks like chance to us is not chance to God. Not one sparrow will fall to the ground apart from your Father (Matt 10:29).

That frees us from two errors: pride when we win, as if our ability guaranteed it, and bitterness when we lose, as if no one were in control.

verseByVerse.quote: For man does not know his time. Like fish that are taken in an evil net, and like birds that are caught in a snare, so the children of man are snared at an evil time, when it suddenly falls upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fish swims into the net without seeing it. So with the accident, the heart attack, the day of death.

Jesus used the same picture for the end of the age. In Noah's day They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all (Luke 17:27). Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect (Matt 24:44). The only preparation for an unknown hour is to be ready at every hour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–18 — The Poor Wise Man Who Saved the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A great king besieged a little city, and a poor, wise man delivered it by his wisdom, Yet no one remembered that poor man (vv. 13-15). Wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's words are despised (v. 16). Quiet words of the wise are better than a ruler's shouting, Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom saves more than strength, and the world rarely thanks the one who saved it.

verseByVerse.quote: I have also seen this example of wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me. There was a little city with few men in it, and a great king came against it and besieged it, building great siegeworks against it. But there was found in it a poor, wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A little city. A parable, perhaps something he saw. Hopeless odds, and the rescuer is not a general but a poor man with wisdom. Scripture has a real example: when Joab besieged the town of Abel, a wise woman called from the city, and the woman went to all the people in her wisdom, and the city was spared (2 Sam 20:16, 22).

Then the sting: the saviour was forgotten. It is hard to read this story without thinking of another poor man. Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Cor 8:9). He came to a world under siege by death and delivered it, and he was despised and rejected by men (Isa 53:3). The Preacher did not have him in view. But the pattern he saw is the pattern of the gospel: God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Cor 1:27). The difference is that this poor man will not be forgotten. God has given him the name above every name.

verseByVerse.quote: But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard. The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the shouting of a ruler among fools. Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is better than might. Yet a wise idea from someone without status is ignored, and a foolish one from someone important applauded. That tells you something about us, not about wisdom.

Heard in quiet. Loudness is not authority. Listen for the quiet voices.

One sinner. Wisdom is stronger than weapons, and one sinner can undo it. Achan's single act of theft brought defeat on all Israel (Josh 7:1). Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? (1 Cor 5:6). It takes a lifetime to build what one act of folly can destroy, and the next chapter opens with the same warning.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>But all this I laid to heart, examining it all, how the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. Whether it is love or hate, man does not know; both are before him.<sup>2</sup>It is the same for all, since the same event happens to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to him who sacrifices and him who does not sacrifice. As the good one is, so is the sinner, and he who swears is as he who shuns an oath.<sup>3</sup>This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that the same event happens to all. Also, the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead.<sup>4</sup>But he who is joined with all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion.<sup>5</sup>For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten.<sup>6</sup>Their love and their hate and their envy have already perished, and forever they have no more share in all that is done under the sun.<sup>7</sup>Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do.<sup>8</sup>Let your garments be always white. Let not oil be lacking on your head.<sup>9</sup>Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your vain life that he has given you under the sun, because that is your portion in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.<sup>10</sup>Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going.<sup>11</sup>Again I saw that under the sun the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to those with knowledge, but time and chance happen to them all.<sup>12</sup>For man does not know his time. Like fish that are taken in an evil net, and like birds that are caught in a snare, so the children of man are snared at an evil time, when it suddenly falls upon them.<sup>13</sup>I have also seen this example of wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me.<sup>14</sup>There was a little city with few men in it, and a great king came against it and besieged it, building great siegeworks against it.<sup>15</sup>But there was found in it a poor, wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man.<sup>16</sup>But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard.<sup>17</sup>The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the shouting of a ruler among fools.<sup>18</sup>Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.
9.overview:
The righteous and the wise are in God's hand, but no one can tell from events whether God's love or hate is upon him (v. 1). The same event, death, comes to righteous and wicked alike, and human hearts are full of evil (vv. 2-3). Yet a living dog is better than a dead lion, for the dead have no more share in what is done under the sun (vv. 4-6).

So the Preacher commands joy: eat bread with joy and drink wine gladly, for God has approved; wear white; enjoy life with the wife you love; and do with your might whatever your hand finds to do, for there is no work in Sheol (vv. 7-10).

The race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong; time and chance happen to all, and people are caught by evil times like fish in a net (vv. 11-12). A poor, wise man delivered a besieged city and was forgotten; wisdom is better than might and weapons, but one sinner destroys much good (vv. 13-18).
9.theology:
God's people are in his hand (v. 1; John 10:29), but his love cannot be read from circumstances. Death comes to all because human hearts are evil (vv. 2-3; Jer 17:9). The dead have no share in this world (vv. 5-6), but those who die in the Lord are with him (Luke 16:22; Phil 1:23; Rev 14:13).

Joy in God's gifts and wholehearted work are commanded, grounded in God's approval (vv. 7-10); for believers that approval rests on Christ (Rom 8:1). What seems chance is governed by God (v. 11; Prov 16:33; Matt 10:29). Wisdom saves, yet the world forgets its deliverers (vv. 13-15), a pattern the gospel echoes in Christ, who became poor to make many rich (2 Cor 8:9).
9.examples:
A promotion is not proof of God's favour, nor a diagnosis of his anger.

The hearse comes for the worshipper and the scoffer alike.

Tonight's supper eaten without wondering whether God is frowning.

The brilliant graduate who cannot find work.

The fish that swims into the net.

The quiet voice in the meeting that no one hears.

10.title: Dead Flies and Sharp Iron

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Little Folly, and Folly in High Places
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stench; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor (v. 1). The wise heart and the fool's heart go different ways, and the fool shows it on the road (vv. 2-3). When a ruler is angry, stay calm (v. 4). The Preacher has seen folly promoted and nobles humbled: slaves on horses, and princes walking on the ground like slaves (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: A little folly spoils much, and a world where folly rules is a world turned upside down.

verseByVerse.quote: Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stench; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 9 ended, one sinner destroys much good. Chapter 10 opens with a picture of the same truth. A jar of expensive perfume, made with care, and a few flies get in and die. Soon the whole jar stinks. It does not take much folly to ruin a great deal of wisdom.

A pastor with thirty years of faithful ministry and one affair. A businessman known for integrity and one fraudulent signature. A father who was patient for years and one explosion of rage that his child never forgets. Reputation takes a lifetime to build, and a little folly outweighs it.

That is a sobering word, and it calls for watchfulness over small things. The flies were small. Which small compromise are you tolerating because it seems too minor to matter?

And if the flies have already spoiled the jar in your life? Reputation may take years to rebuild, and some of it may never come back. But the soul is not ruined beyond repair. Peter denied Christ three times and was restored by him (John 21:15-17). What folly spoils, Christ can forgive and make new.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise man's heart inclines him to the right, but a fool's heart to the left. Even when the fool walks on the road, he lacks sense, and he says to everyone that he is a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Right and left. The right hand in Scripture is the hand of strength and favour (nothing to do with modern politics). Everyone's heart leans somewhere, and the lean decides the direction of the life.

On the road. A fool does not need to announce his folly; he walks down the road, and everyone can see it. A fool's mouth is his ruin (Prov 18:7). Character leaks out in ordinary moments.

verseByVerse.quote: If the anger of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for calmness will lay great offenses to rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Practical counsel for anyone with a boss. When the person over you is angry, the instinct is to storm out or hit back. Stay steady. Calmness is in Hebrew "healing" (ESV note): a calm response heals.

A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger (Prov 15:1). With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone (Prov 25:15). This is not cowardice, nor a call to stay under abuse. It takes more strength to stay calm under anger than to return it, the strength of one who knows that God, not the boss, holds his life.

verseByVerse.quote: There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, as it were an error proceeding from the ruler: folly is set in many high places, and the rich sit in a low place. I have seen slaves on horses, and princes walking on the ground like slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An error from the ruler. Now the problem is at the top: fools get the high offices, and capable people are pushed aside.

Slaves on horses. A world upside down. Isaiah pronounced it as a judgment: I will make boys their princes, and infants shall rule over them (Isa 3:4).

But see what Jesus did with the upside-down world. The Prince of all walked on the ground and rode into Jerusalem on a donkey. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The reversal the Preacher lamented, Christ chose, and by it he turned the world right side up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Risks, Sharp Tools and the Fool's Tongue
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every task has its hazard: the pit, the wall, the stones, the logs (vv. 8-9). If the iron is blunt more strength is needed, but wisdom helps one to succeed (vv. 10-11). The words of a wise man's mouth win him favor, but the lips of a fool consume him; the fool multiplies words about a future he cannot know (vv. 12-14), and his toil wears him out because he does not know the way to the city (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom sharpens the edge of ordinary work and guards the tongue.

verseByVerse.quote: He who digs a pit will fall into it, and a serpent will bite him who breaks through a wall. He who quarries stones is hurt by them, and he who splits logs is endangered by them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pit and wall. Every activity has its risk: the pit, the snake in the old wall. Scripture often uses the pit as a picture of wickedness recoiling on itself: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it (Prov 26:27), and Haman was hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai (Esth 7:10). But here the point seems wider. Every job has its danger.

Stones and logs. The quarryman gets crushed fingers; the woodcutter a slipped axe. That is not a reason to refuse work but to do it with care. Wisdom does not remove all risk. It reduces it.

verseByVerse.quote: If the iron is blunt, and one does not sharpen the edge, he must use more strength, but wisdom helps one to succeed. If the serpent bites before it is charmed, there is no advantage to the charmer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the iron is blunt. Anyone who has cut wood with a dull axe knows this verse. You swing harder, sweat more, and get less done. Stop, sharpen the blade, and the work goes quickly. The ESV notes that the last line may be rendered "wisdom is an advantage for success". Wisdom is the sharpening.

Many people are working harder and harder with a blunt edge: busier, more tired, less effective. The wise thing is sometimes to stop swinging. Rest, pray, learn, plan, ask advice. Time spent sharpening is not time lost.

The serpent charmed too late. Skill must be used at the right time. The right word tomorrow does not help today.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of a wise man's mouth win him favor, but the lips of a fool consume him. The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness, and the end of his talk is evil madness. A fool multiplies words, though no man knows what is to be, and who can tell him what will be after him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gracious words. Win him favor may be rendered "are gracious" (ESV note). The fool talks himself into trouble. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6).

Foolishness to madness. A fool's speech gets worse the longer it goes on. When words are many, transgression is not lacking (Prov 10:19). Anyone who has watched an argument escalate has seen it.

A fool multiplies words, though no man knows what is to be, and who can tell him what will be after him? The fool talks endlessly about the future as if he knew it: the predictions, the plans, the confident forecasts. But no one knows what is to be. James calls the tongue a fire (Jas 3:6), and Jesus warned that on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak (Matt 12:36). How many of your words this week were about things you could not possibly know?

verseByVerse.quote: The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A vivid and slightly comic picture. The fool works hard and wears himself out, and he cannot even find the road into town. All that effort, and he is lost on the obvious path.

Energy without direction exhausts. It is possible to be busy all day and get nowhere because you never asked where you were going. The Preacher means plain good sense, but Christians may add a further thought: the road to the city that matters most is not hidden. The one who said I am the way (John 14:6) leads his people to the city that is to come (Heb 13:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Kings, Sloth, Money and the Whispered Curse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child and princes feast in the morning; happy the land whose princes feast for strength, and not for drunkenness (vv. 16-17). Sloth brings the roof down (v. 18). Bread, wine and money each have their use (v. 19). Even in your thoughts, do not curse the king, for a bird of the air will carry your voice (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Self-control in those who lead, diligence in those who work, and restraint in what we say in private.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child, and your princes feast in the morning! Happy are you, O land, when your king is the son of the nobility, and your princes feast at the proper time, for strength, and not for drunkenness!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, O land. A king immature in years or character, and officials drinking at breakfast. Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink (Isa 5:11). When leaders indulge themselves, the people pay.

Happy are you. And a nation blessed. Feasting is not wrong; eating is for strength. But It is not for kings to drink wine, lest they drink and forget what has been decreed (Prov 31:4-5). Self-control in leaders blesses a whole people, and the same applies to anyone who leads a family or a church; it is the Spirit's fruit, not mere willpower: Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Through sloth the roof sinks in, and through indolence the house leaks. Bread is made for laughter, and wine gladdens life, and money answers everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sloth. A tile slips and is not replaced; years later the ceiling collapses. Sloth works slowly, and its results arrive suddenly. The sluggard's vineyard in Proverbs was all overgrown with thorns, and its stone wall was broken down (Prov 24:31).

So with marriages and souls: the neglected prayer life, the unaddressed conflict.

Money answers everything. In context this sounds like the careless princes speaking. It is partly true: food and wine are for joy, and money solves many practical problems. But the book has shown what money cannot answer: He who loves money will not be satisfied with money (5:10), and it cannot buy the power to enjoy (6:2). Money answers everything except the questions that matter most.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in your thoughts, do not curse the king, nor in your bedroom curse the rich, for a bird of the air will carry your voice, or some winged creature tell the matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A little bird told me": words spoken in private get out. But the verse goes deeper than prudence: the curse begins in the heart before it reaches the lips. Scripture commands honour for those in authority: You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people (Exod 22:28). This does not forbid honest criticism or opposition to injustice. It forbids the private contempt that poisons the one who nurses it.

And there is one listener no one can hide from. Jesus said, whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light (Luke 12:3). Speak in private as you would if the one you speak of were in the room, because the one who judges all things always is.
